**Ariel (collection of poems)**  
A 1965 posthumous collection that includes the famous poems “Lady Lazarus,” “Daddy,” “Tulips,” and “The Moon and the Yew Tree,” establishing Plath as a leading confessional poet.

**The Bell Jar (novel)**  
A semi‑autobiographical novel published under the pen name Victoria Lucas; it follows the mental‑health decline of Esther Greenwood, a stand‑in for Plath herself.

**“Daddy” (poem)**  
One of Plath’s most notorious poems; it uses Holocaust imagery, a “man in black with a Meinkampf look,” and ends with the line “You do / you bastard, I’m through,” addressing her father.

**“Lady Lazarus” (poem)**  
Another signature poem where Plath declares “Out of the ash / I rise,” comparing herself to a phoenix and exploring themes of death, resurrection, and performance.

**Confessional poet**  
Plath is a central figure of the 1950s‑60s confessional movement, writing intensely personal poems that reveal her inner life, mental illness, and relationships.

**Ted Hughes (husband)**  
English poet Ted Hughes married Plath in 1956; their tumultuous relationship and eventual separation heavily influence many of her later poems and the collection *Birthday Letters*.

**Suicide by oven in 1963**  
Plath died by carbon monoxide poisoning in her London kitchen on February 11, 1963, a tragic end that solidified her legacy as a martyr of the confessional genre.

**“Mad Girl’s Love Song” (poem)**  
A short, villanelle‑like poem that repeats the line “I have done it again. One year in every ten,” illustrating Plath’s recurring thoughts of madness and death.

**“The Moon and the Yew Tree” (poem)**  
A gothic‑laden poem that opens with “Fumy spiritous mists / and the light of the mind, cold and planetary,” showcasing Plath’s fascination with death and the natural world.

**“The Colossus” (poem)**  
An early, long poem in which Plath addresses a paternal figure, calling him “a man in black with a Meinkampf look,” and exploring the burden of her father’s memory.

**Victoria Lucas (pseudonym)**  
The name under which Plath published *The Bell Jar*; it reflects her desire to separate her literary identity from her personal one.

**Birthday Letters (collection)**  
A 1998 posthumous collection of poems addressed to Ted Hughes, revealing Plath’s complex feelings about their marriage and serving as a key source for biographical study.
